issue: Does the spousal testimonial privilege include a joint participant exception that lets the government compel a testimonying spouse who is also a co-participant in the charged crime?
provision: Fed. R. Evid. 501; Trammel v. United States, 445 U.S. 40 (1980)

sides.position: Recognizes a joint participant exception to the spousal testimonial privilege for spouses who participated together in the crime
cases: United States v. Van Drunen, 501 F.2d 1393 (7th Cir. 1974)
United States v. Diggs, No. 22-1502 (7th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: Rejects the joint participant exception after Trammel; the privilege belongs to the testifying spouse alone and does not yield where the spouses jointly participated in the crime
cases: United States v. Pineda-Mateo, 905 F.3d 13 (1st Cir. 2018)
In re Grand Jury Subpoena, 755 F.2d 1022 (2d Cir. 1985)
In re Grand Jury, 633 F.2d 276 (3d Cir. 1980)
United States v. Ramos-Oseguera, 120 F.3d 1028 (9th Cir. 1997)
United States v. Diggs, No. 22-1502 (7th Cir. 2023)

this_court: The Seventh Circuit still follows its own Van Drunen recognition of the exception, while the writing urges abandoning it to align with the other circuits; the excerpts do not show the final holding.
quote: That leaves our court isolated on the short end of a lopsided circuit split.
cite: United States v. Tobias Diggs, No. 22-1502 (7th Cir. 2023)
